Learn to follow a no-limit Texas hold’em hand and explain your next decision. Poker Foundations is a free first course: start with the cards, then connect betting, position, the board and possible opposing hands through six core lessons.

For complete beginners and players who know the rules but lose track of the action. Use a deck, counters or paper. The lessons and practice are open to everyone, with no signup or purchase.

Begin with the cards →Know the cards? Start lesson 1

One small task per visit is enough. Try one card-building hand, one scene or a lesson’s short first pass, then pause. The reading estimate covers this whole page, including explanations and the printable card; it is not the length of a class.

What you will learnChoose your starting pointSix-lesson mapRehearse bettingFinish & choose what is next

What you will learn to explain.

  • Which five cards make your hand, and how they compare at showdown.
  • Whose turn it is, which actions are available and how many additional chips a call costs.
  • How position, the changing board and possible opposing hands affect a decision.
  • What a bet is trying to achieve, and which assumptions you still need to check.

Work toward explaining a changed situation with the lesson closed. Opening every page is not a skill test, and this course does not establish readiness to play for money.

Poker guide · Published October 8, 2026

Learn Texas Hold’em with card basics, a best-five hand builder, a guided hand, six connected lessons, varied practice and a private study card.

  • Limped and multiway pots: how to think through live poker

    Poker guide · Published October 15, 2026

    Play against limpers in low-stakes live poker: isolation raises, position, stacks, ranges, a counted cash hand, tournament pressure and solver limits.

  • Multiway pots: count the opponents and the pots.

    Poker guide · Published October 8, 2026

    Distinguish a better call price from a better hand, separate pot eligibility and avoid importing heads-up defense quotas.

  • No-limit Hold’em: rules, decisions and long-term thinking

    Poker guide · Published October 14, 2026

    A comprehensive beginner guide to no-limit Texas hold’em: rules, a counted hand, ranges, pot odds, bet purposes, stack depth, tournaments and a practical study route.

  • Omaha hi-lo: play for a share, not just a low.

    Poker guide · Published October 8, 2026

    Work through legal hand selection, quartering, counterfeiting and pot-share equity with complete fictional examples.

  • Omaha, lowball and mixed games: know which rules changed.

    Poker guide · Published October 8, 2026

    Compare hand construction, low qualifiers and game rotations, then work through an Omaha hi-lo split-pot example.

  • One hand, from deal to showdown.

    Poker guide · Published October 5, 2026

    Follow a complete hand, learn who acts when, and see why winning the pot is different from winning the same amount in profit.

  • One river. Two different stories.

    Poker guide · Published October 6, 2026

    A visual, fictional river exercise: price a call, test the assumed range and reveal two endings without confusing the result with the decision.

  • Pause the hand. Read the situation.

    Poker guide · Published October 5, 2026

    Work through three fictional scenes: calling a raise, a winner that changes twice, and a river decision where price is not the same as equity.

  • Playing poker at Thunder Valley: a first-timer’s guide

    Poker guide · Published October 15, 2026

    Plan your first Thunder Valley poker visit: official room information, WSOP Circuit structures, registration questions, cash waitlists, meals and a private checklist

This is one route through standard 52-card no-limit Texas hold’em: actions and cards, preflop context, the flop, the river, ranges, then betting purpose. Each lesson begins with a limited first pass. Cards, actions and the pot Learn: read your two cards, distinguish checking from calling, find the player whose turn it is and compare the best five cards. The lesson finishes with a complete hand whose chips reconcile. Before moving on: explain what you owe now, rather than repeating the last number announced. Use only your contribution on this betting round when counting a call. Your starting hand in context Learn: describe position, earlier action, effective stacks and the price before asking whether two cards are worth playing. A hand's label leaves out most of the decision. Before moving on: distinguish information you observed from an assumption about hidden cards. Name who still has a turn, including a player who may raise after your call. Your first decisions after the flop Learn: name the made hand and the draw separately, read checks and raises without inventing the opponent's cards, and notice when a helpful shared card improves the other hand too. Before moving on: explain both what your cards make now and what they still need. A possibility to improve is different from a completed hand or a guaranteed win. The turn, river and showdown Learn: rebuild the hand when a new card arrives, recognize that a missed draw can still have showdown value, and distinguish calling a bluff from making one. On the river there is no further community card to rescue a draw. Before moving on: separate the price of a call from evidence that your hand meets it. Before moving on: name a fact and an assumption separately. A check is an observed action; the opponent’s hidden hand remains unknown. The five tasks below are a menu for later study. They are not another beginner course to finish, and the external course is optional. Work at your own pace. None of these activities requires a wager. Keep two headings in your notes: “What I can now explain” and “What I still need to check.” Those notes are more informative than the number of pages opened. Calling costs another 30, making the final pot 120. With no further betting or fees and ordinary showdown equity, the break-even share is 30 / 120 = 25% . Your task is to label the 60, the opponent's 30 and your additional 30. Do not divide by 90 simply because that is what you can see before calling. The free expected-value article below offers a second explanation. For a longer worked exercise, use the pot-odds workshop . 3. Explain a decision before seeing the ending. Your output is one explanation that distinguishes the decision from its result. You do not have to guess the best action. Your output is a statement of the game, betting structure and question. An introductory hold'em rule is not a universal instruction for every game with poker chips. 5. The site listing does not mean every video has been watched or every claim independently reproduced.
